analysis.one_liner: Lets copycat versions of expensive biologic drugs win FDA approval through shorter review, to lower drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: after introduction it was sent to three House committees and a health subcommittee, where it sat until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an abbreviated FDA approval path for "comparable" versions of biologic drugs — the complex, often very expensive medicines made from living cells. Today there is no legal shortcut for these copies (unlike ordinary generic pills), so brand-name biologic makers face no copycat competition even after their patents lapse. The bill would let companies prove their version is comparable with less testing, let the FDA declare a copy "interchangeable" with the original, give the first interchangeable copy a period of market exclusivity, set rules for patent fights, and offer a 50% tax credit for the clinical testing needed to prove interchangeability.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs, such as treatments for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, and anemia, because copycat competition would push prices down the way generics did for ordinary pills. Biologic drug companies that make the copies would also gain a new market, with the first company to prove interchangeability getting a period of exclusivity.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an abbreviated FDA application for a "comparable biological product" — a copy of an already-approved biologic — requiring comparability data rather than a full repeat of the original clinical trials.

Lets an applicant ask the FDA to find its copy "interchangeable" with the original, meaning it could be substituted for the brand drug, and gives the first interchangeable copy a period of market exclusivity.
Adds a 50% tax credit for the clinical testing expenses a company incurs to demonstrate interchangeability, lowering the cost of entering the market.

Sets deadlines for FDA action (a "final action date" about eight months after filing) and restricts petitions and court injunctions that would delay approval, and sets structured timelines and remedies for patent disputes between the brand maker and the copy maker.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug makers, whose exclusive markets would open to copycat competition. The Treasury also bears the cost of the new testing tax credit. Patients face a small safety trade-off if a less-tested copy reaches the market.

drawbacks.text: Biologics are large, complex molecules made in living cells, so a copy can be similar but never identical; critics of abbreviated approval argue that less extensive testing raises safety questions, particularly around immune reactions when a patient switches products.

The market exclusivity for the first interchangeable copy resembles a system that in ordinary generics has sometimes been used to delay competition, and the 50% testing tax credit is a direct subsidy from taxpayers to drug companies.

The bill would still require the copy maker to conduct some clinical studies and settle patent disputes, so savings for patients would arrive more slowly and in smaller amounts than with ordinary generics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for patients is real and large: biologic drugs are among the most expensive medicines, and an approval pathway for copies is the main way competition can reach them. The bill's safety design — requiring comparability data, an optional interchangeability finding, and FDA discretion — is a reasonable version of the trade-off, and the main honest objections are the safety uncertainty inherent in any abbreviated path and the taxpayer subsidy built in for the copy makers. The larger failure is that the bill never advanced at all, so none of these trade-offs was ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Access to Life-Saving Medicine Act on September 29, 2006, joined by Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio.

The bill was referred the same day to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — and on October 2, 2006 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No further action of any kind is recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's core idea — an abbreviated FDA pathway for copies of biologic drugs, with interchangeability determinations and exclusivity for the first interchangeable copy — is laid out in the introduced text.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drug makers kept their exclusive markets and prices untouched, since no competing pathway advanced; patients kept paying brand prices. The bill's own approach resurfaced years later when Congress eventually created a biosimilar pathway, but that was outside this Congress and outside this record.

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an FDA pathway for comparable versions of biologic drugs.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: Original co-introducer, House member from Ohio
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (with Judiciary and Ways and Means)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill beyond referring it to its Subcommittee on Health; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Holder of exclusive licenses on approved biologic drugs
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to allow abbreviated approval of copies of biologic drugs, which would open their markets to competition.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committees of referral never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would end their exclusive control over approved biologic products by letting copycat versions through an abbreviated FDA pathway, so their revenue from top-selling biologics would face competition for the first time. Their interest in keeping exclusivity runs directly against patients' interest in cheaper versions.

The bill creates the legal pathway and a 50% tax credit for the interchangeability testing these companies would need, and gives the first interchangeable copy market exclusivity. Their gain comes from offering patients the same medicine at lower prices.
